title: The Bible
author: Multiple authors
openingText: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Now the earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters. And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the darkness.
about:
The Bible is a library of texts, written over more than a thousand years, in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. It contains creation stories, law codes, history, poetry, prophecy, gospels, letters, and apocalyptic visions. The Hebrew Bible (Old Testament) is the scripture of Judaism; together with the New Testament it is the scripture of Christianity. The Quran also draws on its narratives.

The Bible is the most-read book in human history. It has shaped the languages, literatures, laws, and moral imaginations of much of the world. Reading it cold is encountering the source from which an enormous amount of subsequent culture flows — even for readers who do not share its faith.

angleCards.title: A God who pursues.
angleCards.text: From Genesis to Revelation, the consistent pattern is: humans depart, God calls back. The methods change — covenant, law, prophecy, incarnation — but the direction of the story is always the same. Watch for the pattern and how it develops.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Bible as the story of a God who keeps pursuing people who keep running away — and notice how the nature of that pursuit changes across the whole arc.

angleCards.title: From law to grace.
angleCards.text: The Old Testament is largely a story of requirements and failures. The New Testament argues that the requirements were always pointing toward something else. Reading across the two testaments with this question active is one of the most clarifying ways to read the whole Bible.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the arc from law to grace — what changes between the Old and New Testaments, why it changed, and what the hinge point is.

angleCards.title: God as a character.
angleCards.text: He appears in every book — speaking, acting, judging, relenting, grieving, promising. Reading for character consistency across sixty-six books written over a thousand years is one of the most interesting literary experiments you can attempt.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the character of God across all 66 books — how the portrait develops, deepens, and what remains consistent from Genesis to Revelation.

angleCards.title: The source code of Western thought.
angleCards.text: You cannot fully understand Shakespeare, Dante, Milton, Western law, or modern ethics without knowing this book. Reading it as cultural background — the stories that shaped how the West thinks about justice, sacrifice, redemption, and time — is entirely legitimate and enormously useful.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Bible as the foundational text of Western civilisation — understanding the stories, laws, and ideas that shaped everything that came after, regardless of belief.

cast.name: God
cast.description: The only figure who appears across all sixty-six books. His character shifts in tone across the testaments — but the core attributes (creator, pursuer, judge, redeemer) remain. He is the subject of every book in the Bible even when unnamed.

cast.name: Moses
cast.description: He leads an entire people out of slavery and then spends forty years trying to bring them to a place they keep refusing to trust. He never enters the promised land himself. His greatness and his failure are inseparable.

cast.name: David
cast.description: Shepherd, warrior, poet, king, adulterer, murderer, father of a ruined household. The Bible presents him as the greatest king of Israel and spends almost as much time on his failures as his victories. The Psalms are largely his.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.description: He writes in the 8th century BCE about events that the New Testament will claim came true seven hundred years later. His language — servant songs, peaceable kingdom, light in darkness — shapes the way the whole tradition speaks about hope.

cast.name: Jesus
cast.description: The New Testament's claim is that everything in the Old was pointing toward him. Whether or not you believe that, he is the figure around whom the entire second half of the Bible is organised — and who remade the world more than anyone else in history.

cast.name: Paul
cast.description: A trained rabbi who persecuted Christians and then had a conversion experience that changed him completely. His letters make up a large portion of the New Testament and constitute the first systematic theology of the new faith.

whyItMatters.title: The Source of Western Imagination
whyItMatters.body: Almost every theme in Western literature — from the Odyssey forward — is in conversation with the Bible. Hamlet, Paradise Lost, Crime and Punishment, Moby Dick, Beloved — all written by readers of the Bible, all responding to it.

whyItMatters.title: Multiple Voices, Not One
whyItMatters.body: The Bible is not one book. It contains poetry that contradicts the law next to it, gospels that disagree about Jesus's last words, prophets who quarrel with kings. Reading it as a library of voices rather than a single uniform text is closer to what it actually is.

whyItMatters.title: A Book About a People
whyItMatters.body: Most of the Bible is the story of a particular people — Israel — and what happens to them: liberation, kingdom, exile, return, occupation, hope. The relationship between God and a people in history is the book's central concern.
